blocks.body:
Suppose you measure a quantity at four times and expect it to grow linearly. Four points almost never lie on one line, so the system "line passes through all four points" has no solution. What should you do? The method of least squares, used by Legendre and Gauss around 1800 to fit planetary orbits, says: choose the line that makes the sum of squared errors as small as possible.

The answer has a clean geometric meaning. The best approximation to $b$ by vectors of the form $Ax$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $b$ to the column space of $A$. This page develops that picture using [[inner-products]] and [[linear-maps]], derives the normal equations, and explains why numerical software solves them via the QR factorisation instead.

blocks.title: Projecting onto a line
blocks.body:
Start with one direction $a\neq0$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ and a vector $b$. The closest multiple $\hat c\,a$ to $b$ is the one for which the error $b-\hat c a$ is perpendicular to $a$: $a\cdot(b-\hat ca) = 0$, so
$$\hat c = \frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a},\qquad p = \frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a}\,a.$$
For $a = (1,1,1)$ and $b = (1,2,6)$ this gives $\hat c = 9/3 = 3$, $p = (3,3,3)$ and error $b-p = (-2,-1,3)$, which is perpendicular to $a$. Notice that $\hat c=3$ is the mean of the entries of $b$: the mean is the least-squares fit of a constant.

Why perpendicular? For any other multiple $ca$, Pythagoras gives $\|b-ca\|^2 = \|b-p\|^2 + (c-\hat c)^2\|a\|^2 \ge \|b-p\|^2$. The same argument works for any subspace.

blocks.title: Best approximation by orthogonal projection
blocks.body:
Let $W$ be a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$. There is a unique $p\in W$ with $b-p\perp W$ (the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto $W$), and for every $w\in W$ with $w\neq p$,
$$\|b-w\| > \|b-p\|.$$
If $W$ is the column space of an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, then $p = A\hat x$ exactly when $\hat x$ solves the normal equations $A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$. These always have a solution, and the solution is unique if and only if the columns of $A$ are linearly independent.

Minimality: if $b-p\perp W$ and $w\in W$, then $p-w\in W$ is perpendicular to $b-p$, so $\|b-w\|^2 = \|b-p\|^2+\|p-w\|^2$, which exceeds $\|b-p\|^2$ unless $w=p$. This also shows $p$ is unique, since any other candidate would have to be strictly closer and strictly farther at once.

Normal equations: $b - Ax\perp W$ means $b-Ax$ is perpendicular to each column of $A$, i.e. $A^{\mathsf{T}}(b-Ax) = 0$.

Existence: every subspace $W$ is the column space of some matrix $A$ (take a basis of $W$ as columns), so it suffices to treat that case. $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ and $A$ have the same null space, because $A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax = 0$ implies $\|Ax\|^2 = x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax = 0$. By rank–nullity they have the same rank, so the column space of $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ (contained in that of $A^{\mathsf{T}}$) equals the column space of $A^{\mathsf{T}}$, which contains $A^{\mathsf{T}}b$. Hence the normal equations are solvable, and any solution gives a projection $p = A\hat x$. The solution is unique iff $\operatorname{null}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A) = \operatorname{null}A = 0$, i.e. iff the columns are independent.

blocks.title: The projection matrix
blocks.body:
When the columns of $A$ are independent, $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ is invertible and
$$\hat x = (A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}b,\qquad p = Pb,\quad P = A(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}.$$
The matrix $P$ depends only on the subspace, not on the choice of basis columns. It is symmetric, $P^{\mathsf{T}} = P$, and idempotent, $P^2 = P$: projecting twice changes nothing. Conversely every symmetric idempotent matrix is the orthogonal projection onto its column space. The complementary matrix $I-P$ projects onto the orthogonal complement, and $b = Pb + (I-P)b$ splits $b$ into "explained" and "error" parts. For a single column $a$, $P = aa^{\mathsf{T}}/(a^{\mathsf{T}}a)$, recovering the line case.

blocks.title: Fitting a line to four points
blocks.body: Find the least-squares line $y = C + Dt$ through the made-up data points $(0,1), (1,3), (2,4), (3,4)$, and check that the error vector is perpendicular to the columns.
blocks.solution:
The system $C + Dt_i = y_i$ is $Ax = b$ with
$$A = \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\\1&3\end{pmatrix},\quad x = \begin{pmatrix}C\\D\end{pmatrix},\quad b = \begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\4\\4\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $A^{\mathsf{T}}A = \begin{pmatrix}4&6\\6&14\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^{\mathsf{T}}b = \begin{pmatrix}12\\23\end{pmatrix}$. Solving $4C+6D = 12$, $6C+14D = 23$ gives $D = 1$, $C = 3/2$. The best line is $y = \tfrac32 + t$.

The fitted values are $\tfrac32,\tfrac52,\tfrac72,\tfrac92$, and the error $e = b - A\hat x = (-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12)$. Its dot product with $(1,1,1,1)$ is $0$ (errors sum to zero) and with $(0,1,2,3)$ is $\tfrac12+1-\tfrac32 = 0$. The minimum sum of squared errors is $\|e\|^2 = 1$. Note that what is minimised is the sum of squared vertical distances, not perpendicular distances to the line.

blocks.title: Gram–Schmidt and the QR factorisation
blocks.body:
Projection is easy when the basis of $W$ is orthonormal: if $q_1,\dots,q_n$ are orthonormal, then $p = \sum_j (q_j\cdot b)\,q_j$, with no system to solve. Gram–Schmidt produces such a basis from independent columns $a_1,\dots,a_n$: subtract from $a_k$ its projections onto $q_1,\dots,q_{k-1}$ and normalise. Since each $a_k$ is a combination of $q_1,\dots,q_k$, this is a factorisation
$$A = QR,$$
where $Q$ is $m\times n$ with orthonormal columns ($Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I$) and $R$ is $n\times n$ upper triangular with positive diagonal; $r_{jk} = q_j\cdot a_k$.

Substituting into the normal equations gives $R^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}QR\hat x = R^{\mathsf{T}}Q^{\mathsf{T}}b$, and since $R^{\mathsf{T}}$ is invertible,
$$R\hat x = Q^{\mathsf{T}}b,$$
a triangular system solved by back-substitution. The projection matrix becomes simply $P = QQ^{\mathsf{T}}$.

The reason to prefer this numerically: the condition number of $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ is the square of that of $A$. If $A$ has condition number $10^8$, forming $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ in double precision (about 16 digits) can destroy every significant digit, while QR works with $A$ itself. Library routines compute $Q$ and $R$ by Householder reflections, which are more stable than classical Gram–Schmidt; the result is the same factorisation up to the signs of the columns of $Q$ and the rows of $R$.

blocks.title: The same fit via QR
blocks.body: Compute the QR factorisation of the matrix $A$ from the line-fitting example and use it to recover $C$ and $D$.
blocks.solution:
First column: $a_1 = (1,1,1,1)$ has length $2$, so $q_1 = \tfrac12(1,1,1,1)$ and $r_{11} = 2$.

Second column: $a_2 = (0,1,2,3)$, $r_{12} = q_1\cdot a_2 = 3$, and $a_2 - 3q_1 = (-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$, of length $\sqrt5$. So $r_{22} = \sqrt5$ and $q_2 = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(-\tfrac32,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$. Thus
$$R = \begin{pmatrix}2&3\\0&\sqrt5\end{pmatrix}.$$
Next $Q^{\mathsf{T}}b = (q_1\cdot b,\ q_2\cdot b) = (6,\ \sqrt5)$, because $q_2\cdot b = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt5}(-\tfrac32-\tfrac32+2+6) = \tfrac{5}{\sqrt5}$. Back-substitution: $\sqrt5\,D = \sqrt5$ gives $D=1$, then $2C+3 = 6$ gives $C = \tfrac32$, as before.

blocks.title: Least squares for functions
blocks.body: Find real numbers $a, b$ minimising $\displaystyle\int_0^1 (x^2 - a - bx)^2\,dx$, and find the minimum value.
blocks.solution:
Work in the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with inner product $\langle f,g\rangle = \int_0^1 fg\,dx$. We want the orthogonal projection of $x^2$ onto $W = \operatorname{span}\{1,x\}$. The normal equations say the error $x^2-a-bx$ is orthogonal to $1$ and to $x$:
$$\int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)\,dx = \tfrac13 - a - \tfrac b2 = 0,\qquad \int_0^1(x^2-a-bx)\,x\,dx = \tfrac14-\tfrac a2-\tfrac b3 = 0.$$
Solving, $b = 1$ and $a = -\tfrac16$. The best line is $x - \tfrac16$, and the error is $e(x) = x^2 - x + \tfrac16$. Since $e\perp W$, the minimum is
$$\int_0^1 e(x)^2\,dx = \int_0^1 e(x)\,x^2\,dx = \tfrac15 - \tfrac14 + \tfrac1{18} = \tfrac1{180}.$$
The same reasoning in infinite dimensions is the projection theorem in [[hilbert-spaces]]; the error polynomial $x^2-x+\frac16$ is, up to a constant, the second Legendre polynomial shifted to $[0,1]$.

blocks.title: Rank-deficient problems and the pseudoinverse
blocks.body: If the columns of $A$ are dependent, the projection $p$ is still unique but $\hat x$ is not: any vector of $\operatorname{null}A$ can be added. The standard choice is the solution of smallest norm, which is the unique solution lying in the row space of $A$. It is $\hat x = A^+b$, where $A^+$ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse, computed most reliably from the [[svd]]: if $A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}$ then $A^+ = V\Sigma^+U^{\mathsf{T}}$, with $\Sigma^+$ inverting the nonzero singular values. For full column rank, $A^+ = (A^{\mathsf{T}}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf{T}}$.

- The least-squares solution does not solve $Ax=b$; it solves $A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$. If $b$ happens to lie in the column space, the two agree.
- $Q^{\mathsf{T}}Q = I$ but $QQ^{\mathsf{T}}\neq I$ when $Q$ is not square; $QQ^{\mathsf{T}}$ is the projection $P$.
- Projection matrices are not invertible (unless $P = I$): information perpendicular to $W$ is lost.
- Forming $A^{\mathsf{T}}A$ squares the condition number; use QR or the SVD for ill-conditioned problems.
- Regressing $y$ on $t$ and regressing $t$ on $y$ give different lines, because they minimise different (vertical versus horizontal) errors.
- Squared errors make the fit sensitive to outliers; a single wild data point can tilt the line considerably.

In statistics, least squares with a probability model for the errors becomes [[linear-regression]], where $\hat x$ is the vector of fitted coefficients and $\|e\|^2$ the residual sum of squares. The minimum-norm solution and the best low-rank approximations both come from the [[svd]]. Minimising $\|Ax-b\|^2$ is the simplest problem in [[convex-optimisation]], and it can also be attacked iteratively by [[gradient-descent]], which is how very large fits are done. The best-approximation property of orthogonal projection explains why [[fourier-series]] partial sums are optimal in the mean-square sense, and polynomial least-squares fitting is a close relative of the [[interpolation-quadrature|interpolation]] methods of numerical analysis.

1. Find the least-squares solution of $x_1 + x_2 = 1$, $x_1 - x_2 = 1$, $x_1 = 3$.
2. Show that if $P$ is the projection onto $W$, then $I-P$ is the projection onto $W^\perp$, and $(I-P)P = 0$.
3. Fit a parabola $y = C+Dt+Et^2$ to the points $(-1,2),(0,0),(1,1),(2,5)$ by the normal equations.
4. Show that if $A$ has orthonormal columns then the least-squares solution is $\hat x = A^{\mathsf{T}}b$, and explain the result geometrically.
